items.stem: Which of the following best describes "closed system"?
options: A system in which matter cannot enter or leave, although energy can be exchanged
The value of the equilibrium expression calculated using concentrations at any moment, not necessarily at equilibrium
Industrial conditions chosen to balance equilibrium yield, rate, cost and safety
A reaction that releases heat to the surroundings (ΔH negative)
items.answer: A system in which matter cannot enter or leave, although energy can be exchanged
items.markingKey: A. "closed system" is a system in which matter cannot enter or leave, although energy can be exchanged.

items.stem: What is the relationship between Kc for a reaction and Kc for its reverse?
items.answer: They are reciprocals.
items.markingKey: A. 1/Kc.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the concentrations at equilibrium remain constant even though reactions are still occurring.
items.answer: The forward and reverse reactions proceed at the same rate, so each species is formed as fast as it is used up. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The forward and reverse reactions proceed at the same rate, so each species is formed as fast as it is used up. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Kc for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) is 54 at 700 K. State Kc for HI(g) ⇌ ½H₂(g) + ½I₂(g) at 700 K.
For the dissociation of dinitrogen tetroxide, N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), an equilibrium mixture contains (mol dm⁻³): [N₂O₄] = 1.39, [NO₂] = 0.25. Calculate Kc at this temperature.
items.markingKey: B. Kc = [NO₂]² / [N₂O₄] (M1); substitution (M1); Kc = 0.0450 (A1).

items.stem:
Omar studied the equilibrium between hydrogen, violet iodine vapour and colourless hydrogen iodide: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). Values of Kc were measured at several temperatures.

T / K | Kc
600 | 70.8
650 | 61.2
698 | 54.3
750 | 48.5

(a) Write the expression for Kc. [1]
(b) Deduce, with a reason, the sign of ΔH for the forward reaction. [2]
(c) At 650 K the equilibrium concentrations of H₂ and I₂ are both 0.0023 mol dm⁻³. Calculate the equilibrium concentration of HI. [2]
(d) Explain why Kc has no units for this reaction. [1]
(e) Predict the effect of doubling the total pressure on the position of equilibrium. [2]
items.answer: (a) Kc = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) (b) negative (exothermic): Kc decreases as temperature increases, so the reverse reaction is favoured by heating. (c) 0.018 mol dm⁻³ (d) The concentration terms cancel: (mol dm⁻³)²/(mol dm⁻³)². (e) No effect: there are equal numbers of gas molecules on each side.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] correct expression (1). (b) [2] negative (1); Kc falls with T (1). (c) [2] [HI] = √(Kc × [H₂][I₂]) = √(61.2) × 0.0023 (M1) = 0.018 mol dm⁻³ (A1). (d) [1] unit analysis (1). (e) [2] no shift (1); 2 mol gas on each side (1).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "position of equilibrium".
items.answer: The relative amounts of reactants and products present at equilibrium
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the relative amounts of reactants and products present at equilibrium. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Why does an equilibrium mixture appear unchanging?
options: The reactants have been used up.
The forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates.
items.answer: The forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates.
items.markingKey: D. Dynamic.

items.stem: "At equilibrium both the forward and backward reactions stop." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Both reactions continue at equal rates (dynamic equilibrium).
items.markingKey: Both reactions continue at equal rates (dynamic equilibrium). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a static equilibrium and a dynamic equilibrium.
items.answer: In a static equilibrium nothing is changing; in a dynamic equilibrium forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
items.markingKey: In a static equilibrium nothing is changing; in a dynamic equilibrium forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: At a certain temperature Kc = 0.0218 for CO(g) + 2H₂(g) ⇌ CH₃OH(g). What is the value of Kc for the equation with all coefficients halved at the same temperature?
items.markingKey: C. Coefficients ×½ → √Kc = 0.148.

items.stem: For the Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), an equilibrium mixture contains (mol dm⁻³): [N₂] = 0.11, [H₂] = 1.35, [NH₃] = 0.83. Calculate Kc at this temperature.
items.markingKey: Kc = [NH₃]² / [N₂][H₂]³ (M1); substitution (M1); Kc = 2.55 (A1).

items.stem: For N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), Kc = 3.15 × 10¹² at a given temperature. Which statement is correct?
options: The equilibrium mixture contains mostly products.
The equilibrium mixture contains mostly reactants.
Significant amounts of both reactants and products are present.
items.answer: The equilibrium mixture contains mostly products.
items.markingKey: B. Kc ≫ 1; K says nothing about rate.

items.stem: "The concept of dynamic equilibrium applies only to chemical reactions in closed laboratory vessels." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: The idea extends far beyond laboratory vessels, though true equilibrium strictly needs a closed system.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: equilibrium requires a closed system; textbook examples are closed vessels. Arguments against: phase equilibria (liquid–vapour) and solubility equilibria are dynamic; biological and environmental systems (O₂–haemoglobin, CO₂–ocean) behave similarly; steady states in open systems resemble equilibria. Supported judgement: The idea extends far beyond laboratory vessels, though true equilibrium strictly needs a closed system. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "Le Chatelier’s principle".
items.answer: If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, the position of equilibrium shifts to partially counteract (minimise) the change
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: if a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, the position of equilibrium shifts to partially counteract (minimise) the change. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the effect of temperature on equilibrium and the effect of pressure on equilibrium.
items.answer: Temperature changes both the position and the value of K; pressure changes only the position (for reactions with different numbers of gas moles), not K.
items.markingKey: Temperature changes both the position and the value of K; pressure changes only the position (for reactions with different numbers of gas moles), not K. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Maya writes: "Adding more reactant increases the value of Kc." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Kc is unchanged; the position shifts right until the ratio returns to Kc.
items.markingKey: Kc is unchanged; the position shifts right until the ratio returns to Kc. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: For esterification of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH(l) + C₂H₅OH(l) ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅(l) + H₂O(l), ΔH = −2 kJ mol⁻¹, predict and explain the effect on the equilibrium yield of CH₃COOC₂H₅ when more CH₃COOH is added.
items.answer: Yield increases: the system uses up some of the added reactant.
items.markingKey: yield increases (1); the system uses up some of the added reactant (1).

items.stem: Which conditions give the highest equilibrium yield of NO₂ in 2NO(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), ΔH = −114 kJ mol⁻¹?
items.answer: low temperature and high pressure
items.markingKey: A. Exothermic forward reaction → low T; gas moles 3 → 2 → high p.

items.stem: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), ΔH = +52 kJ mol⁻¹. What happens if the pressure is decreased by increasing the volume at equilibrium?
options: The position shifts to the right and Kc decreases.
The position does not change and Kc is unchanged.
The position shifts to the right and Kc increases.
The position shifts to the left and Kc increases.
items.answer: The position does not change and Kc is unchanged.
items.markingKey: B. More gas moles favoured (Δn = 0); only temperature changes Kc.

items.stem:
Kenji studied the dissociation of colourless dinitrogen tetroxide into brown nitrogen dioxide: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). Values of Kc were measured at several temperatures.

T / K | Kc / mol dm⁻³
273 | 5.55 × 10⁻⁴
298 | 0.00460
323 | 0.0275
398 | 1.52

(a) Write the expression for Kc. [1]
(b) Deduce, with a reason, the sign of ΔH for the forward reaction. [2]
(c) At 273 K the equilibrium concentration of N₂O₄ is 0.16 mol dm⁻³. Calculate the equilibrium concentration of NO₂. [2]
(d) Explain why Kc has units of mol dm⁻³ for this reaction. [1]
(e) Predict and explain the colour change when the volume of the container is halved at constant temperature. [2]
items.answer: (a) Kc = [NO₂]²/[N₂O₄] (b) positive (endothermic): Kc increases with temperature, so the forward reaction is favoured by heating. (c) 0.0094 mol dm⁻³ (d) There is one more concentration term in the numerator than the denominator: (mol dm⁻³)²/(mol dm⁻³). (e) Initially darker (concentration doubles), then becomes paler as equilibrium shifts left towards fewer gas molecules; Kc unchanged.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] correct expression (1). (b) [2] positive (1); Kc rises with T (1). (c) [2] [NO₂] = √(Kc × [N₂O₄]) = √(5.55 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.16) (M1) = 0.0094 mol dm⁻³ (A1). (d) [1] unit analysis (1). (e) [2] shift left – fewer moles of gas (1); immediate darkening then partial fading (1).

items.stem: In the Contact process, 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −196 kJ mol⁻¹, conditions of about 450 °C, 2 atm and a V₂O₅ catalyst are used. (a) Predict the effect of increasing temperature on the yield and on Kc. (b) Explain why a higher pressure is not used. (c) Explain the role of V₂O₅. (d) Suggest why excess air is used.
items.answer: (a) yield and Kc decrease (exothermic). (b) conversion already ~99 % at low pressure; high pressure costly. (c) increases rate, equilibrium reached faster, no effect on yield. (d) increases [O₂], shifting the position right and using all the more valuable SO₂.
items.markingKey: (a) yield and Kc decrease (exothermic). (b) conversion already ~99 % at low pressure; high pressure costly. (c) increases rate, equilibrium reached faster, no effect on yield. (d) increases [O₂], shifting the position right and using all the more valuable SO₂.

items.stem: Why is an iron catalyst used in the Haber process?
options: To increase the rate at which equilibrium is reached.
items.answer: To increase the rate at which equilibrium is reached.
items.markingKey: C. Catalysts affect rate only.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "yield"?
options: A system in which matter cannot enter or leave, although energy can be exchanged
Industrial conditions chosen to balance equilibrium yield, rate, cost and safety
A reaction that can proceed in both the forward and reverse directions
The amount of product obtained, often expressed as a percentage of the theoretical maximum
items.answer: The amount of product obtained, often expressed as a percentage of the theoretical maximum
items.markingKey: D. "yield" is the amount of product obtained, often expressed as a percentage of the theoretical maximum.

items.stem: Explain why Le Chatelier’s principle predicts but does not explain shifts in equilibrium.
items.answer: It describes the direction of the shift; the explanation lies in changes in the relative rates of the forward and reverse reactions (or Q versus K).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It describes the direction of the shift; the explanation lies in changes in the relative rates of the forward and reverse reactions (or Q versus K). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In terms of rates, why does adding reactant shift an equilibrium to the right?
options: The forward rate increases temporarily until the rates are equal again.
items.answer: The forward rate increases temporarily until the rates are equal again.
items.markingKey: B. Rates rebalance.

items.stem: State and explain the effect of adding a small amount of NaOH(aq) to 2CrO₄²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l).
items.answer: OH⁻ removes H⁺; equilibrium shifts left; colour changes from orange to yellow.
items.markingKey: OH⁻ removes H⁺; equilibrium shifts left; colour changes from orange to yellow.

items.stem: Which conditions give the highest equilibrium yield of NH₃ in N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹?
items.answer: low temperature and high pressure
items.markingKey: B. Exothermic forward reaction → low T; gas moles 4 → 2 → high p.

items.stem: For the dissociation of phosphorus pentachloride, PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), ΔH = +88 kJ mol⁻¹, predict and explain the effect on the equilibrium yield of PCl₃ when more PCl₅ is added.
items.answer: Yield increases: the system uses up some of the added reactant.
items.markingKey: yield increases (1); the system uses up some of the added reactant (1).

items.stem: A student claims: "Increasing the temperature always shifts the equilibrium to the right." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction, which may be either forward or reverse.
items.markingKey: Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction, which may be either forward or reverse. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Removing the product continuously is the best way to increase the yield of an equilibrium reaction."
items.answer: Removing product is highly effective where separation is easy, but the best method depends on the system.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shifts the equilibrium right without changing K; used for NH₃ (liquefied) and esters (distilled off). Arguments against: not always physically possible; requires energy for separation; changing T, p or excess reagent can be cheaper. Supported judgement: Removing product is highly effective where separation is easy, but the best method depends on the system. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: "Removing the product continuously is the best way to increase the yield of an equilibrium reaction." Discuss.
items.answer: Removing product is highly effective where separation is easy, but the best method depends on the system.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shifts the equilibrium right without changing K; used for NH₃ (liquefied) and esters (distilled off). Arguments against: not always physically possible; requires energy for separation; changing T, p or excess reagent can be cheaper. Supported judgement: Removing product is highly effective where separation is easy, but the best method depends on the system. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: At equilibrium, how are Q and K related?
items.answer: Q = K
items.markingKey: D. Definition.

items.stem: Distinguish between equilibrium concentrations and initial concentrations.
items.answer: Initial concentrations are those before reaction; equilibrium concentrations are initial values adjusted by the changes (x) that occur as equilibrium is reached.
items.markingKey: Initial concentrations are those before reaction; equilibrium concentrations are initial values adjusted by the changes (x) that occur as equilibrium is reached. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why can equilibrium concentrations never be negative in an ICE calculation?
options: A species cannot react beyond the amount present, so x is limited by the reactant amounts.
items.answer: A species cannot react beyond the amount present, so x is limited by the reactant amounts.
items.markingKey: A. Physical constraint.

items.stem: For CO(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO₂(g) + H₂(g), Kc = 0.734. A mixture contains [CO] = 1.50, [H₂O] = 0.69, [CO₂] = 0.52, [H₂] = 0.73 mol dm⁻³. In which direction does the reaction proceed?
options: no net reaction – the system is at equilibrium
it cannot be predicted without knowing ΔH
items.answer: towards products (forward)
items.markingKey: A. Q = 0.367 < Kc → towards products (forward).

items.stem: For A(g) ⇌ B(g) + C(g), Kc = 8.51 × 10⁻⁶ at 500 K. Starting with [A] = 1.00 mol dm⁻³, calculate [B] at equilibrium, stating the approximation used.
items.answer: 0.00292 mol dm⁻³
items.markingKey: Kc = x²/(1.00 − x) ≈ x²/1.00 because K is very small (M1); x = √(8.51 × 10⁻⁶ × 1.00) (M1) = 0.00292 mol dm⁻³ (A1).

items.stem:
A student mixed 0.176 mol of ethanoic acid, 0.203 mol of ethanol and a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid in a sealed tube and left it for a week at 298 K. The mixture was quickly made up to 250.0 cm³ with ice-cold water (to stop further reaction), and 25.00 cm³ portions were immediately titrated with 0.250 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. After allowing for the sulfuric acid, the mean titre due to ethanoic acid was 20.67 cm³.
CH₃COOH(l) + C₂H₅OH(l) ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅(l) + H₂O(l)

(a) Calculate the amount of ethanoic acid remaining at equilibrium. [2]
(b) Determine the equilibrium amounts of ethanol, ethyl ethanoate and water. [2]
(c) Calculate Kc for the reaction. [2]
(d) State the role of the sulfuric acid. [1]
(e) Predict the effect on the yield of ethyl ethanoate of adding more ethanol. [1]
items.answer: (a) 0.0517 mol (b) ethanol 0.0787 mol; ester and water 0.124 mol each (c) 3.80 (d) catalyst – speeds up attainment of equilibrium (e) The yield increases: equilibrium shifts right to use up the added ethanol.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ICE table"?
options: A reaction that can proceed in both the forward and reverse directions
A table of Initial, Change and Equilibrium amounts or concentrations used to calculate equilibrium compositions
A reaction that releases heat to the surroundings (ΔH negative)
The value of the equilibrium expression calculated using concentrations at any moment, not necessarily at equilibrium
items.answer: A table of Initial, Change and Equilibrium amounts or concentrations used to calculate equilibrium compositions
items.markingKey: B. "ICE table" is a table of Initial, Change and Equilibrium amounts or concentrations used to calculate equilibrium compositions.

items.stem: Elena writes: "In an ICE table the changes are always equal for every species." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The changes are in the ratio of the stoichiometric coefficients.
items.markingKey: The changes are in the ratio of the stoichiometric coefficients. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain when it is reasonable to assume that x is negligible in an equilibrium calculation.
items.answer: When K is very small (e.g. < 10⁻³) relative to the initial concentrations, so very little reacts and [A]₀ − x ≈ [A]₀; the result should be checked (x < 5 % of [A]₀).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: When K is very small (e.g. < 10⁻³) relative to the initial concentrations, so very little reacts and [A]₀ − x ≈ [A]₀; the result should be checked (x < 5 % of [A]₀). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In an ICE table for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, if N₂ changes by −x, what is the change for NH₃?
items.markingKey: B. Mole ratio 1 : 2.

items.stem: Equal initial concentrations of H₂ and I₂, each 0.100 mol dm⁻³, are heated: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), Kc = 64.0. Calculate the equilibrium concentration of HI.
items.answer: 0.160 mol dm⁻³

items.stem: Equal initial concentrations of H₂ and I₂, each 0.200 mol dm⁻³, are heated: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), Kc = 46.0. Calculate the equilibrium concentration of HI.
items.answer: 0.309 mol dm⁻³

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "ICE-table calculations accurately predict real equilibrium mixtures."
items.answer: They give good estimates under ideal conditions but are approximations for concentrated or non-ideal systems.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: based on the equilibrium law, which holds well for dilute solutions and ideal gases. Arguments against: concentrations should be activities: deviations at high concentration; K values are temperature-specific and often approximate; approximations (small x) introduce error. Supported judgement: They give good estimates under ideal conditions but are approximations for concentrated or non-ideal systems. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: 2.00 mol of H₂ and 2.00 mol of I₂ are heated in a 1.00 dm³ flask until equilibrium: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), Kc = 49.0. (a) Construct an ICE table. (b) Calculate the equilibrium concentration of each species. (c) Calculate the percentage of H₂ converted. (d) Predict the effect of adding 1.00 mol of HI at equilibrium, using Q.
items.answer: (a) I: 2, 2, 0; C: −x, −x, +2x; E: 2 − x, 2 − x, 2x. (b) √49 = 7 = 2x/(2 − x) → x = 1.56: [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.444, [HI] = 3.11 mol dm⁻³. (c) 77.8 %. (d) Q rises above K → reverse reaction until Q = K.
items.markingKey: (a) I: 2, 2, 0; C: −x, −x, +2x; E: 2 − x, 2 − x, 2x. (b) √49 = 7 = 2x/(2 − x) → x = 1.56: [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.444, [HI] = 3.11 mol dm⁻³. (c) 77.8 %. (d) Q rises above K → reverse reaction until Q = K.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "thermodynamic control"?
options: The extent of reaction determined by the relative stability (ΔG) of reactants and products rather than by rates
The state of a reversible reaction in a closed system in which the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations remain constant
The value of the equilibrium expression (product concentrations raised to their coefficients divided by reactant concentrations raised to theirs) at a given temperature
The Gibbs energy change for a reaction with all species in their standard states; related to K by ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K
items.answer: The extent of reaction determined by the relative stability (ΔG) of reactants and products rather than by rates
items.markingKey: A. "thermodynamic control" is the extent of reaction determined by the relative stability (ΔG) of reactants and products rather than by rates.

items.stem: Distinguish between ΔG⦵ and ΔG.
items.answer: ΔG applies to the actual conditions (and is zero at equilibrium); ΔG⦵ refers to standard states and fixes the value of K.
items.markingKey: ΔG applies to the actual conditions (and is zero at equilibrium); ΔG⦵ refers to standard states and fixes the value of K. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why is ΔG zero for a system at equilibrium?
options: There is no further tendency for net change in either direction.
ΔH and ΔS are both zero.
items.answer: There is no further tendency for net change in either direction.
items.markingKey: B. Equilibrium = minimum G.

items.stem: Calculate K at 298 K for a reaction with ΔG⦵ = −10.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
A student claims: "If ΔG⦵ is negative, the reaction goes to completion." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A negative ΔG⦵ means K > 1, so products predominate, but some reactants remain unless K is extremely large.
items.markingKey: A negative ΔG⦵ means K > 1, so products predominate, but some reactants remain unless K is extremely large. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "A negative ΔG⦵ guarantees that a reaction will be observed."
items.answer: ΔG⦵ shows feasibility only; whether reaction is observed depends on kinetics and conditions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: negative ΔG⦵ means products are favoured at equilibrium. Arguments against: high activation energy may make it imperceptibly slow (diamond → graphite); non-standard conditions change ΔG. Supported judgement: ΔG⦵ shows feasibility only; whether reaction is observed depends on kinetics and conditions.

items.stem: Which equation links ΔG⦵ and the equilibrium constant?
items.answer: ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K
items.markingKey: C. Data booklet.

items.stem: Explain the significance of the sign of ΔG⦵ for the position of equilibrium.
items.answer: ΔG⦵ < 0 gives K > 1 (products favoured); ΔG⦵ > 0 gives K < 1 (reactants favoured); ΔG⦵ = 0 gives K = 1.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: ΔG⦵ < 0 gives K > 1 (products favoured); ΔG⦵ > 0 gives K < 1 (reactants favoured); ΔG⦵ = 0 gives K = 1. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A reaction has ΔG⦵ = +5 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Which statement is correct?
options: K is slightly less than 1; noticeable amounts of products form.
items.answer: K is slightly less than 1; noticeable amounts of products form.

items.stem: At 400 K the equilibrium constant of a reaction is 6.07 × 10⁻⁵. What is the sign of ΔG⦵ and which species predominate at equilibrium?
items.answer: ΔG⦵ is positive; reactants predominate
items.markingKey: C. K < 1 → ln K < 0 → ΔG⦵ positive.

items.stem: For PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), ΔG⦵ = +40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ at 400 K. Calculate the equilibrium constant at this temperature.
items.markingKey: B. ln K = −ΔG⦵/RT = −(+40700)/(8.31 × 400) = −12.2 (M1, J conversion); K = 4.81 × 10⁻⁶ (A1); reactants predominate (R1).

items.stem:
A student mixed 0.205 mol of ethanoic acid, 0.154 mol of butan-1-ol and a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid in a sealed tube and left it for two weeks at 298 K. The mixture was quickly made up to 250.0 cm³ with ice-cold water (to stop further reaction), and 25.00 cm³ portions were immediately titrated with 0.400 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. After allowing for the sulfuric acid, the mean titre due to ethanoic acid was 21.50 cm³.
CH₃COOH(l) + C₄H₉OH(l) ⇌ CH₃COOC₄H₉(l) + H₂O(l)

(a) Calculate the amount of ethanoic acid remaining at equilibrium. [2]
(b) Determine the equilibrium amounts of butan-1-ol, butyl ethanoate and water. [2]
(c) Calculate Kc for the reaction. [2]
(d) Explain why the volume of the mixture does not need to be known to calculate Kc. [1]
(e) Explain why ice-cold water was used. [1]
items.answer: (a) 0.0860 mol (b) butan-1-ol 0.0350 mol; ester and water 0.119 mol each (c) 4.70 (d) There are equal numbers of moles on each side, so the volume terms cancel in the expression. (e) Cooling and dilution slow the reaction so the equilibrium composition is not changed before titration.

items.stem: For steam reforming of methane, CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g), ΔH⦵ = +206 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = +215 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate ΔG⦵ and K at 298 K and at 1200 K. items.answer: forward, to form more products

items.stem: Distinguish between thermodynamic stability and kinetic stability.
items.answer: Thermodynamic stability depends on ΔG (relative energies of reactants and products); kinetic stability depends on Ea (how fast change occurs).

items.stem: Explain the effect of increasing pressure on the yield of SO₃ in 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g).
items.answer: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules (3 → 2), so the position shifts right and the yield of SO₃ increases; in practice the yield is already high at about 1–2 atm.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a dynamic equilibrium and a static equilibrium.
items.answer: In a static equilibrium nothing is changing; in a dynamic equilibrium forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
items.markingKey: In a static equilibrium nothing is changing; in a dynamic equilibrium forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "If Q is less than K, the reaction is at equilibrium." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Q < K means the system is not at equilibrium; the forward reaction proceeds until Q = K.

items.stem: Explain why a reaction with a negative ΔG⦵ may not occur at a noticeable rate.
items.answer: ΔG⦵ shows that products are favoured at equilibrium, but says nothing about the activation energy; a high Ea makes the reaction very slow (kinetic stability).

items.stem: For 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), ΔH = −57 kJ mol⁻¹. What happens if more N₂O₄ is added at equilibrium?

items.stem: Briefly explain why the changes in an ICE table must follow the mole ratio of the equation.
items.answer: The amounts of each species that react or form are fixed by stoichiometry: for aA + bB → cC the changes are −ax, −bx and +cx.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a moderate temperature (about 450 °C) is used in the Haber process although a lower temperature gives a higher yield.
items.answer: The forward reaction is exothermic, so low T increases yield, but the rate would be too slow; 450 °C is a compromise between acceptable yield and rate (with an iron catalyst).
